item.title: Record-breaking 2025 Iberian fire season was three times larger due to climate change
item.description: The latest global State of Wildfires report, co-led by the University of East Anglia, shows that the extreme fire-prone weather experienced across Spain and Portugal in 2025 was three times more likely due to human-caused climate change, and the area burned was three times larger. The paper is published in Earth System Science Data. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study Links Climate And Violence: Peru skeletons show low conflict; ritual sacrifice stays distinct
item.description: Throughout history, ancient communities in Peru's Lambayeque Valley confronted significant flooding and food scarcity. Interestingly, despite these hardships, instances of interpersonal violence were notably infrequent. Research indicates that only a tiny percentage of skeletal remains revealed signs of conflict. Instead, these resilient societies cleverly adapted, capitalizing on marine resources to weather environmental challenges. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: "Por la economía, para reducir el coste de vida", el slogan a favor de la acción climática en la COP31
item.description: El mensaje, que se repite en la conferencia anual de la ONU, refleja el esfuerzo por captar la atención de Estados y Gobiernos que enfrentan conflictos y crisis que han puesto al cambio climático en un segundo plano en las prioridades. Según el secretario general, se debe alcanzar consenso en torno a cuatro principios: el fin de la dependencia de los combustibles fósiles, la adaptación a un mundo más cálido, elevar el apoyo a los países vulnerables y promover la cooperación frente al conflicto. Fuente: France 24 - Español.

item.description: Brandywine Creek is now revitalized and flowing freely, thanks to the successful removal of Hoffman's Mill Dam. The removal, executed by a coalition of organizations, was meticulously planned to safeguard local wildlife, promoting ecological balance and enhancing recreational prospects for residents. item.title: Why are Britain's streets still so polluted? Because the car industry dinosaurs do what they like, and politicians let them | George Monbiot
item.description: The transition to electric vehicles should be moving apace, but it is not. And why? Incompetence, expedience and cowardice This is how it works. An industry puts tremendous effort into resisting change: lobbying governments, mobilising the media, pouring money into junktanks . It argues that a transition would threaten jobs, or damage the national interest, or harm poor people, while what it really fears is the cost of retooling its plants or developing new protocols. Then, when the inevitable cliff edge approaches, it whines that change is coming too soon. For reasons beyond its control, it… Fuente: The Guardian - Environment.

item.title: Cacti are severely threatened by drought in a warming world
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03496-z Forecasts of the effects that climate change will have on biodiversity typically rely on long-term climate averages while excluding extreme events. Projections that include severe drought predict that a majority of the 993 cactus species assessed will see large losses of suitable climatic area: more than 25% of species could lose at least 80% of it by 2100. Fuente: Nature.

item.title: Archives reveal how climate memories may reset with each generation
item.description: The collective memory of floods and droughts influences where people settle, how they build and how they prepare for the next climatic extreme. Over decades, that memory can fade, and communities may return to places that once proved dangerous. How such memory decayed over centuries is hard to observe because the climate past societies experienced is usually known only from their own records. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A new method for tracking climate change and air pollution
item.description: Two papers by Prof. Thomas A. Weber develop a rank-based method to track environmental change. They apply the idea to follow Geneva's warming climate, and generalize the approach to quantify shifts in spatial air-pollution exposure across Switzerland. The method compares observations with a historical baseline and shows how accounting for where people live changes the assessment of air-quality improvements. Fuente: Phys.org.

This year’s meeting – called the Conference of the Parties, or Cop31 – comes after a year of climate-induced heatwaves and other disasters. As she arrived at the meeting venue in Antalya, Turkey, Thunberg, 23, said climate change is “threatening everything” and that “everything and everyone we love is at stake”. “We... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: This small Alaska town is swamped by cruise ship visitors every summer. But what happens when they all go home?
item.description: Skagway’s 1,100 permanent residents are caught between a boom time – when the ships bring more than a million tourists – and a lull in winter October comes to the small Alaska coastal town of Skagway like a sigh. The shops that were bustling throughout the crazed tourist season are reducing their opening hours or beginning to close. The hordes of employees sleeping in overcrowded bunkhouses are leaving or have left. The crowds of cruise passengers who have filled the streets since April, wearing lanyards emblazoned with the names of their ships, have dwindled to a trickle. item.title: Climate crisis could push 141 million more women into extreme poverty
item.description: More than one in three women and girls worldwide – roughly 1.5 billion – live in so-called “climate hotspots”, where high exposure to hazards such as cyclones and droughts combine with insecure jobs and deep gender inequality. Fuente: UN News.

item.title: How did these shrines survive a tsunami?
item.description: When the 2011 tsunami devastated Japan’s coast, patches of forest were left standing amid the destruction. Many surrounded Shinto shrines, ancient chinju-no-mori, or “guardian forests”, that appeared to protected them when disaster struck. item.title: Tuesday briefing: The world is falling short on climate action. Can Cop31 change that?
item.description: In today’s newsletter: As global leaders gather in Turkey for the UN climate summit, both doubts and hope surround what the annual talks can achieve Good morning. item.description: A Michigan business's drainage changes sent excess rainwater onto a neighbouring property, causing years of flooding and damage to the house and garage. item.title: Global fossil fuel emissions set to fall in 2026, but total CO2 keeps rising
item.description: Global fossil fuel emissions are projected to fall in 2026 as renewable energy and electric vehicles gain ground, but rising emissions from deforestation threaten to push total CO2 emissions to a new record. Scientists warn that the world's remaining carbon budget for limiting warming to 1.5°C could be exhausted in less than four years, even as a lasting decline in emissions appears increasingly within reach. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Smart use of trees and crops brings best yield
item.description: Cultivating crops—such as wheat, barley and rye—alongside rows of trees is a system of agroforestry that is known as "alley-cropping." It serves many functions: in addition to enhancing ecosystems and biodiversity, it can also counteract the negative effects of growing crops in treeless open land. The advantages of alley-cropping come from the interaction between trees and crops, resulting in improved soil quality, reduced wind erosion, enhanced nutrient cycling, and climate change mitigation through increased carbon capture. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: The Venetian lagoon is home to "barene" – salt marshes made of vegetation and mud, which play an important role against the effects of climate breakdown. They absorb CO2 and can store it long term in the soil, even more efficiently than land forests. But erosion and rising sea levels are threatening these natural ramparts.
